articles.title: Cobalt’s Silent Cartel: China, Kinshasa and the DRC Export Quota - Geopolitical Monitor
articles.summary: Cobalt’s Silent Cartel: China, Kinshasa and the DRC Export Quota  Geopolitical Monitor
articles.full_text:
- China refined 78 percent of the world’s cobalt in 2024 while mining almost none of it, according to the International Energy Agency.
- Kinshasa’s export quota moved the payable value of Congolese cobalt hydroxide from about 55 percent of the metal price to 100 percent, shifting margin from Chinese refiners to producers in the DRC.
- Cobalt is a byproduct at the large Chinese-operated copper mines, so with copper near record prices those operators can absorb the cobalt squeeze while expanding the metal that matters more to their economics.
Zijin Mining, one of China’s largest mining companies, disclosed in its half-year report that flooding at the Kamoa-Kakula copper complex in the Democratic Republic of the Congo could cut its share of 2026 output by as much as 57,000 tonnes, an announcement that helped keep copper above $14,000 per tonne, near its record high. The disclosure shows how concentrated the exposure has become: a production problem at a single Congolese mine, operated through a Chinese joint venture, now moves the global price of the metal underpinning electrification and AI infrastructure.
That concentration extends beyond copper. In cobalt, where the DRC supplies roughly 70 percent of global mined output, the combination of Kinshasa’s export quota regime and Chinese dominance of both mining and refining has produced a structure that behaves like a cartel without any party having declared one. Examining how that structure allocates volume, price, and risk clarifies what Western supply-chain diversification is actually competing against.
How Kinshasa’s Cobalt Export Quota Works
The DRC produced about 220,000 tonnes of cobalt in 2024, while China refined 78 percent of global output despite mining almost none domestically, according to the International Energy Agency. Chinese firms bridge that gap through direct ownership: CMOC, the world’s largest cobalt producer, Zijin, and Huayou Cobalt anchor a corporate presence that, by 2022, held stakes in 15 of 19 Congolese cobalt mines, with Chinese state-owned enterprises and policy banks controlling an estimated 80 percent of output. Beijing is also Kinshasa’s largest bilateral creditor under the 2007 infrastructure-for-minerals framework.

articles.title: Portfolio Diplomacy Pays Ethiopia, the 18th BRICS Summit, and the Economics of Balanced Engagement - ifa.gov.et
articles.summary: Portfolio Diplomacy Pays Ethiopia, the 18th BRICS Summit, and the Economics of Balanced Engagement  ifa.gov.et
articles.full_text:
Summit-sideline diplomacy is often treated as a courtesy layer on top of real statecraft: a run of handshakes, communiqués and photographs that supplements the harder work done through embassies and dedicated state visits. The 18th BRICS Summit, held in New Delhi on 12–13 September 2026, invites a different reading.
Within a single year, Prime Minister Dr. Abiy Ahmed held discussions with leaders from numerous Western nations on the sidelines of the G20 summit in Johannesburg on 22–23 November 2025, and then held a further series of bilateral discussions with leaders of BRICS in New Delhi. Taken together, the two engagements show a country speaking with several centres of global influence at once, without asking any of them to choose on its behalf. The visits by influential world leaders to Ethiopia over the past two years point the same way: Ethiopia has emerged as a significant centre of diplomatic gravity.
This brief reads that pattern as portfolio diplomacy, and argues that New Delhi shows it converting breadth of engagement into specific, recorded multilateral backing for Ethiopia’s national priorities.
Portfolio Diplomacy, Defined
This brief uses the term to describe the deliberate spreading of a state’s engagement across several centres of influence, so that no single relationship has to carry the full weight of its national priorities. The government describes its own approach in similar terms: cost-effective, centred on national interest, grounded in an understanding of global realities, balanced and free from partisan bias, rooted in the philosophy of Medemer (synergy), and committed to inclusivity.
Three features give the concept substance. The first is efficiency. A diplomatic mission to three or four countries in a single year would demand considerable expense, time and preparation; a leaders’ summit compresses much of that work into a few days of concentrated bilateral contact. The second is discipline. Ethiopia’s discussions with numerous BRICS member nations in New Delhi demonstrated its commitment to neutrality while it pursued its national interests, and holding those two commitments together is itself a diplomatic success. The third is agenda-setting. Ethiopia brought its national agendas, above all access to the sea, to the forefront of these conversations, which can fairly be counted a major achievement.
What New Delhi Delivered
The clearest return came in the New Delhi Declaration. On trade, member states reaffirmed their commitment to “a rules-based, open, transparent, fair, predictable, inclusive, equitable, non-discriminatory, and consensus-based multilateral trading system, with the World Trade Organization (WTO) at its core,” and added direct support for Ethiopia’s accession, expressly endorsing East Africa’s largest economy.
Transport followed. The bloc declared: “We support the sole candidacy of Ethiopia, representing the African continent, for election to an expanded seat on the Council of the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO).” The bloc unanimously backed Ethiopia as the only candidate put forward by the African Union, recognising its extensive aviation experience.1 On climate, in support of African leadership in the global green transition, the bloc fully endorsed Ethiopia’s bid to host and chair the COP32 climate conference in Addis Ababa in 2027, and pledged joint support for its preparations.
The fourth outcome was political. Access to the sea and the reform of international multilateral institutions were placed firmly on the agenda. The Prime Minister made clear that Ethiopia’s economic survival depends on sea access, and underlined the nation’s unwavering commitment to pursuing it only through bilateral negotiation and peaceful means. The Declaration itself reiterated the bloc’s commitment to reforming multilateral institutions, strengthened support for African integration into the global economy, and placed Ethiopia at the centre of discussions on trade, transport and climate.
A bilateral track ran alongside the summit. The Prime Minister’s meetings with leaders of BRICS member and partner nations focused on strengthening mutually beneficial partnerships in trade, investment, defense, technology and digitalization.3 Consultations with China advanced the two nations’ all-encompassing strategic partnership and cooperation on trade, investment and the expanded BRICS framework. Talks with India covered defense cooperation, technology transfer, capacity building, digital infrastructure and mineral development. Discussions with Russia addressed security, trade, investment, science and technology, and education, while those with Kazakhstan and Malaysia centred on digitalization, renewable energy, industrial productivity, and regional peace and stability. Consultations with Iran reflected the same balanced, inclusive and Medemer-inspired approach.
The Limits of a Declaration
A cautious reader will note that a declaration records support; it does not itself deliver outcomes. WTO accession, an ICAO Council seat and the hosting of COP32 each run through their own formal processes, and bilateral consultations express intent rather than binding commitment. The observation is fair, but it understates what a collective, publicly recorded endorsement provides.
Ethiopia now holds a documented, bloc-wide statement of support on three files that matter directly to its economy and its standing, and it can cite that record in every subsequent negotiation and election. The relevant test is therefore not whether New Delhi settled these questions, which it did not and was never meant to, but whether it improved Ethiopia’s starting position on each. On that measure the summit was productive.
Ethiopia’s Stake, and the Road from Here
For Ethiopia, the stake is larger than any single endorsement. Engagement in New Delhi opens new trade and investment prospects, widens the range of financial and technological partners beyond conventional Western financial institutions, and strengthens the country’s influence internationally. Because the same government also engaged Western leaders at the G20, this is best read as diversification rather than realignment.
Four practical steps follow. First, Ethiopia should turn the WTO endorsement into accession momentum, drawing on the stated support of BRICS members in its bilateral trade discussions. Second, the ICAO candidacy and the COP32 hosting bid deserve dedicated diplomatic attention, since recorded support becomes a real outcome only when it is followed up, member by member. Third, the consultations with China, India, Russia, Kazakhstan, Malaysia and Iran should be translated into sequenced follow-up work on trade, investment, technology and digitalization, with clear institutional ownership. 
Fourth, Ethiopia should keep its Western and BRICS tracks in deliberate balance, and continue to present its case for access to the sea as a matter for bilateral negotiation and peaceful means, consistent with the Prime Minister’s stated position. The trade-off is bandwidth. A wider portfolio demands a deeper bench of negotiators and planners, and follow-through will test institutional capacity more than summitry does.
A Diplomacy That Keeps Its Balance
New Delhi did not create Ethiopia’s diplomatic approach; it revealed how that approach now works. By engaging Western leaders in Johannesburg and BRICS leaders in New Delhi within a single year, the government has shown that neutrality and national interest can be pursued together. The result is a portfolio of relationships broad enough to carry Ethiopia’s priorities on trade, transport, climate and access to the sea, and balanced enough that no partner is asked to give up another. That is the practical meaning of portfolio diplomacy, and on the evidence of these two days in New Delhi, it is working.

1. “BRICS Summit Endorses Ethiopia’s WTO Bid, Backs Key Global Roles for Addis Ababa.” The Reporter, September 12, 2026.
2. “BRICS Summit Backs Ethiopia’s Global Diplomatic, Economic Agenda.” Ethiopian News Agency (ENA), Addis Ababa, September 14, 2026.
3. Office of the Prime Minister of Ethiopia. Communications on the Prime Minister’s bilateral meetings, 18th BRICS Summit, New Delhi, September 2026.
4. BRICS. New Delhi Declaration. 18th BRICS Summit, New Delhi, September 12–13, 2026.

articles.title: Egyptian minister rejects Israeli concerns over Sinai railway project - Middle East Monitor
articles.summary: Egyptian minister rejects Israeli concerns over Sinai railway project  Middle East Monitor
articles.full_text:
Egyptian Transport Minister Kamel El-Wazir said on Wednesday that Egypt’s expansion of transport infrastructure in North Sinai and the reopening of railway lines to reconnect the peninsula with the rest of Egypt are part of efforts to develop the area. His remarks came in response to concerns over the projects reported by Hebrew media.
Speaking on Egyptian television on Wednesday evening, El-Wazir said he was focused on restoring the Sinai railway and extending it to Bir al-Abd, then to Al-Arish and later Taba, alongside the Suez Canal tunnels he oversaw while serving as head of the Armed Forces Engineering Authority.
He said the projects aimed to reconnect Sinai with the rest of Egypt, adding: “Why are they upset? Have we attacked anyone? This is our land and we have the right to develop it.”
El-Wazir said a logistics corridor between Al-Arish and Taba would help revive Sinai by linking the ports of Al-Arish on the Mediterranean and Taba on the Red Sea, allowing goods from Arab countries to be transported alongside goods arriving from India and China through the Arab Gulf states.
“What are they worried about? Does the train fire bullets? The train carries passengers or goods and is a development corridor,” he said.
Asked whether Israel feared the Egyptian projects could undermine Israeli plans for an alternative to the Suez Canal by transporting goods by rail, El-Wazir replied: “What is done is done. We are developing our land and this is our right. If this thwarts their plans, they should see what we are doing.”
Israeli reports have expressed concern over the pace of development in Sinai and Egypt’s construction of new transport infrastructure, particularly railway lines, saying it could lead to logistical and demographic changes that strengthen Egypt’s presence along the border.
Israeli platform Natziv Net said the Sinai railway project, which stretches for 500 km to link Egypt’s main logistics hub with the interior of the peninsula and eventually Taba, had raised strategic concerns in Tel Aviv, describing it as a major shift extending beyond civilian infrastructure.

articles.title: Africa Gas & LNG Summit 2026 to Bring Investment and Local Value Into Focus in Maputo - Africa Oil+Gas Report
articles.summary: Africa Gas & LNG Summit 2026 to Bring Investment and Local Value Into Focus in Maputo  Africa Oil+Gas Report
articles.full_text:
PARTNER CONTENT
Three-day Maputo summit will bring together government, industry and investors to examine the next phase of Africa’s gas and LNG development.
MAPUTO, MOZAMBIQUE, September 2026 – The Africa Gas & LNG Summit (AfGLNG) will take place in Maputo from 11–13 November 2026, bringing together government leaders, energy executives, investors and industry experts to examine how Africa can convert its gas resources into investment, infrastructure and wider economic opportunity.
Held at the Joaquim Chissano International Conference Centre, the summit will take place under the official patronage of H.E. Daniel Chapo, President of the Republic of Mozambique, and the Ministry of Mineral Resources and Energy. President Chapo is scheduled to deliver the presidential welcome on the opening day, while Hon. Estevão Pale, Minister of Mineral Resources and Energy, will also take part in key discussions across the programme, underscoring the high-level government support for the summit.
AfGLNG 2026 is hosted by the Associação de Conteúdo Local de Moçambique (ACLM), with Empresa Nacional de Hidrocarbonetos, E.P. (ENH), Mozambique’s national hydrocarbons company and government equity partner in the country’s LNG projects, and the Instituto Nacional de Petróleo (INP), the regulator overseeing Mozambique’s licensing and contract compliance, as strategic partners.
The summit comes as African gas projects face critical investment and development decisions, while governments look to secure greater economic value from the continent’s resources. Mozambique alone illustrates the scale of that shift: Mozambique LNG, led by TotalEnergies, is a US$20 billion development projected to produce approximately 13 million tonnes per year; Rovuma LNG, led by ExxonMobil and Eni, is licensed for 18 Mtpa; Coral South FLNG has been exporting gas since 2022 as Africa’s first deepwater floating LNG project; and the US$6–7 billion Coral North FLNG expansion will double that output by 2028. With Africa emerging as an increasingly important part of the global gas supply chain, AfGLNG 2026 will focus not only on new investment, but also on how gas development can support infrastructure, industrialisation and broader economic benefit across the continent.
A central focus of the conference will be where investment goes next. Regional sessions will examine opportunities across Mozambique, North Africa, West Africa and Southern Africa, including Senegal and Mauritania’s Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project, Nigeria’s expanding LNG and pipeline infrastructure, and new gas developments in Congo, Angola and Tanzania, giving delegates a broader view of the different markets, project environments and investment priorities shaping gas development across the continent.
An Africa Energy Ministers’ Forum will bring together nine African energy ministries to discuss policy, investment and regional cooperation, while the wider programme will connect these policy discussions with the commercial and project-level issues facing the sector.
The programme will also look at what is needed to move projects forward. A dedicated FID session will examine the path towards Final Investment Decision, alongside discussions on finance, LNG infrastructure, gas-to-power, industrialisation and the wider African LNG value chain.
Local content will form another major strand of the summit. A dedicated SME and Entrepreneurs session will explore supplier development, access to finance and practical opportunities for African businesses to participate in the industry’s growth. The focus reflects a wider theme running through the summit: ensuring that gas development creates opportunities not only through exports, but also through local supply chains, enterprise development and economic participation.
The opening programme will also feature an Energy Leaders’ Dialogue under the theme “The African Gas Opportunity: Turning Resources into Prosperity,” focused on turning natural resources into long-term economic value.
Confirmed participants also include Rudêncio Morais, Chairman of ENH; Nazário Bangalane, Chairman of INP; Dr Elthon Chemane, Chairman of ACLM Mozambique; Farid Ghezali, Secretary General of the African Petroleum Producers’ Organisation (APPO); Ranti Omole, CEO of Radial Circle; and Eng. Elizabeth Rogo, President & CEO of Tsavo Oilfield Services, Kenya.
A parallel technical track will run alongside the executive conference on Day 2. The summit will also feature an international exhibition, an opening-day exhibition tour and cocktail reception, and networking opportunities throughout the three-day programme, creating additional space for direct engagement between government, industry, investors and service providers.
Further information, including sponsorship and exhibition opportunities, is available at africagaslng.com.

AfGLNG 2026 takes place 11–13 November 2026 at the Joaquim Chissano International Conference Centre, Maputo, Mozambique, under the official patronage of H.E. articles.title: Uganda Seeks Stronger Cross-Border Mining Ties as Tanzanian Firms Attend Kampala Conference - Nilepost
articles.summary: Uganda Seeks Stronger Cross-Border Mining Ties as Tanzanian Firms Attend Kampala Conference  Nilepost
articles.full_text:
Uganda's High Commissioner to Tanzania, Amb Col (Rtd) Fred Mwesigye, has urged mining firms in the region to form joint partnerships, arguing that small-scale operators working alone struggle to attract the capital and skills they need to grow.
Amb Mwesigye was speaking at the 15th Annual Mineral Wealth Conference and Expo at Speke Resort Munyonyo, Kampala, where the Uganda High Commission in Dar es Salaam brought 18 Tanzanian mining companies and organisations. The two-day conference, which ran from 29 to 30 September, was themed around unlocking Africa's next mining powerhouse. It was organised by the Uganda Chamber of Energy and Minerals and the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development.
"Our primary objective is to create a platform where African practitioners in the industry of mining come together and discuss and maybe create joint partnerships," Amb Mwesigye said. "When they are together they are stronger. But when we operate individually we are weaker."
The delegation list shared by the mission includes the Tanzania Chamber of Mines, AngloGold Ashanti Tanzania, Shanta Mining Co. Ltd, Tembo Nickel Corporation, Faru Graphite Corporation, Perseus Mining's Sotta Mining Corporation, TRX Gold Corporation's Buckreef Gold, Petra Diamonds' Williamson Diamonds, Lifezone Metals' Kabanga Nickel Project and Peak Rare Earths' Ngualla Project, among others. Amb Mwesigye said participants had also come from Zambia and Walawi.
He said the visiting firms were showing interest in partnerships rather than stand-alone investments. "Through partnerships they become stronger and can then attract resources to add value, to increase their capacity in mining," he said. "Individually nobody looks at them. But when they are together people will be attracted to look at them."
Amb Mwesigye was one of several Ugandan envoys at the conference. The diplomats came from missions in Africa, Europe, Asia and the Americas. Amb Richard Kabonero, head of regional economic cooperation and economic and commercial diplomacy, led the delegation.
The other missions represented included the Uganda Embassy in Brussels, led by Amb Mirjam Blaak, and the Uganda Embassy in Moscow, represented by Amb Moses Kizige. Amb Musazi represented the Uganda Embassy in Havana, and the Uganda Embassy in Ankara, Türkiye, also took part. Prof Joyce Kikafunda, Uganda's High Commissioner in New Delhi, was also part of the delegation.
Their attendance falls under the Ministry of Foreign Affairs' economic and commercial diplomacy programme. The programme aims to build economic and commercial diplomacy into mission work plans and to link diplomacy directly to economic transformation. At recent review meeting for Uganda's missions in Asia and the Pacific in Foshan, China, Amb Kabonero told envoys that diplomacy must now produce measurable economic results tied to the country's tenfold growth strategy.
Humphrey Asiimwe, chief executive of the Uganda Chamber of Energy and Minerals, said the Ministry of Foreign Affairs had helped invite investors through Uganda's embassies abroad. He said the conference had drawn more than 1,000 delegates from 30 countries, with 81 companies exhibiting.
Mineral value addition was a central topic at the conference. Sidronius Opolot Okaasai, the Minister of State for Energy, said the government had taken a deliberate decision to stop the export of unprocessed minerals. He also said it had put in place a policy and legal framework to support local processing, including licensing incentives for investors who set up refineries and processing plants in Uganda.
He urged investors to process minerals in Uganda instead of exporting raw ore. "Process it, refine it, add value to it, and the money is there," he said.
Mr Okaasai, who stood in for the Minister of Energy and Mineral Development, Dr Monica Musenero, said the ministry plans a minerals sub-sector with three arms: a policy arm within the ministry, a standalone regulator, and a national mining company, which he said was now in place. He said the government would also increase funding for exploration of critical minerals, including phosphate and rare earth elements.
Mr Asiimwe said the fourth National Development Plan prioritises mineral value addition. He said the Wagagai gold mine in eastern Uganda had begun operating since last year's conference and, by his account, produces 1.5 tonnes of 99.98% pure gold a year.
The European Union's ambassador to Uganda, Jan Sadek, said the EU would have mobilised more than €25m in grants for the sector once ongoing and planned projects were counted together. He said the bloc supports Uganda's ambition to stop exporting unprocessed minerals.
Amb Mwesigye said the high commission follows up with participants after such conferences to check whether what they learnt is put into practice.
He said the mission had previously taken Ugandan small and medium-scale miners to Tanzania, including to Geita, to learn from their Tanzanian counterparts. He described Tanzania as ahead of Uganda in organising small-scale miners, saying it licenses them, organises them and creates a market for their minerals. The trips are made with the chamber of mines, which he said then works to organise Ugandan miners, help them get licences and add value.
Asked about tariff and non-tariff barriers affecting the sector between the two countries, Amb Mwesigye acknowledged they exist. "Definitely they are there," he said. He added that the mission identifies them through conferences and engages stakeholders, tackling legal barriers through legal channels and seeking to ease financial ones for small-scale miners.
He said Tanzanians had initially been cautious about closer economic ties. "We keep telling Tanzanians that we are actually real brothers, and they should open up like we have opened up," he said. He added that continued interaction was removing "artificial fears" and bringing people closer.
The mining focus mirrors the shape of trade between the two countries, which is dominated by gold. Speaking at a Uganda-Tanzania trade mission in 2025, Amb Mwesigye put bilateral trade in 2024 at about $2.23 billion, up from $1.36 billion in 2023. He said Uganda's exports to Tanzania were $185 million against imports of $2.0 billion, an imbalance he said needed to be addressed.
Uganda Revenue Authority data for the 2024/25 financial year shows Tanzania accounted for Shs12.46 trillion, or 21.94 per cent, of Uganda's total imports, making it the country's largest single supplier ahead of China, India, the United Arab Emirates and Kenya.
Adam Mugume, Research Director at the Bank of Uganda, attributed the surge mainly to gold and precious minerals, with other Tanzanian goods such as rice estimated at $100 million to $150 million. Bank of Uganda import data cited by Tanzania's The Citizen shows Uganda imported goods worth $2.26 billion from Tanzania between January and October 2025, against $1.35 billion from Kenya.
Figures published by the Ministry of Finance show Uganda's largest trade deficit in the East African Community in the second quarter of 2024/25 was with Tanzania, at $497 million.
Diplomatic engagement between Kampala and Dar es Salaam has intensified this year. President Yoweri Museveni visited Tanzania twice in 2026, in February and again on 5–6 August, for talks with President Samia Suluhu Hassan.
Tanzania's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the August talks would review resolutions from the Fifth Session of the Tanzania-Uganda Joint Permanent Commission held in March 2026 and include the signing of an energy cooperation memorandum.
Beyond the East African Crude Oil Pipeline, the two governments are pursuing a proposed natural gas pipeline from Tanzania to Uganda, a refined petroleum products pipeline to Tanga, port expansion and railway projects.
Amb Mwesigye also gave an update on Kiira Motors Corporation, the state-owned bus maker in Jinja, which he said had drawn interest from Tanzanian buyers. He said he visited the company about a week ago and found it had built the capacity to produce buses but was manufacturing according to demand.
He said markets had opened in Tanzania, Zambia, Mozambique and Malawi, each with different specifications, though most buyers were interested in electric buses. Amb Mwesigye is also accredited to Zambia, Mozambique, Malawi, Comoros and Mauritius from his base in Dar es Salaam.
"I have appealed to the government, the minister of finance, that they should not leave that giant lying idle. They should put in money in order to compete with the Chinese producers, because the China government puts funds in these companies," he said.
In November 2025, the company drove its Kayoola E-Coach through Tanzania, including Dodoma, on an electric expedition from Kampala to Cape Town.
Amb Mwesigye, a retired colonel and former Member of Parliament for Nyabushozi County, has served as High Commissioner to Tanzania since December 2021.

articles.title: Port Washington yard expansion that LIRR called a bottleneck enters design - Railway Supply
articles.summary: Port Washington yard expansion that LIRR called a bottleneck enters design  Railway Supply
articles.full_text:
The MTA has moved the Port Washington LIRR station renewal into design, a project that also extends two nearby yard tracks so the railroad can base more trains there.
The Metropolitan Transportation Authority said on September 28, 2026, that the station and yard project on the Port Washington Branch is now in design. It describes the work as a design-build project. The preliminary design award comes from the MTA’s 2020-2024 Capital Program. Later construction phases are expected to draw on the 2025-2029 Capital Program. The announcement gave no cost, construction schedule or contractor.
MTA Construction & Development President Jamie Torres-Springer said the upgrades are meant to put the station in a state of good repair and to make service on the branch more reliable.
Station works planned at Port Washington
Safety, passenger circulation and accessibility shape the station scope. Ramps, curb cuts, sidewalks and accessible parking will be rebuilt. Inside and out, the station building will get upgrades, including a reconfigured and larger restroom. Its roof and the plaza canopy will be replaced.
New platforms will come with new canopies and a new structure beneath them. An enclosed crossing with new elevators will take the place of the existing pedestrian overpass. Stairs and the ADA ramp will also be renewed. Communication systems and security cameras are due for upgrades, and the lighting will switch to LED.
Two yard tracks for longer trains
The second part of the project lengthens two tracks in the yard near the station. According to the MTA, this will let the LIRR keep longer trains at this end of the branch without getting in the way of maintenance, inspections and car cleaning.
Also in the yard package are rehabilitation of the trainmen’s building, updates to the employee facility and its parking, and improvements at three parking lots: LIRR Yard, South Bayles Avenue and Haven Avenue.
Port Washington Yard capacity since 2022
In September 2022 the LIRR released revised draft timetables for the branch ahead of the Grand Central Madison opening. Catherine Rinaldi, then the railroad’s interim president, named more track capacity at Port Washington Yard as the key to future service increases. She described the long-sought yard project as “the bottleneck to having more service on the branch.” Those drafts still added 10 weekday trains, for 103 a day, without any extra storage space at the yard. In November 2025, MTA Construction & Development told the MTA board’s Capital Program Committee that it was advancing procurement for the Port Washington Station Renewal design, following approval of the 2025-2029 program.

articles.full_text:
Russian Export Center to Lead Business Mission to AEW 2026 in Cape Town
The Trade Representation of the Russian Federation in South Africa, together with the Russian Export Center, will organize an international business mission of Russian companies and industry associations to African Energy Week (AEW) 2026 in Cape Town from October 13–15. The mission will provide a platform for participating Russian companies to engage with African energy stakeholders and explore commercial opportunities across the continent.
The delegation will form part of AEW 2026, taking place October 12–16, bringing Russian businesses into discussions around Africa’s energy development, industrialization and infrastructure investment. The Trade Representation, which operates as the trade and economic branch of the Russian Embassy in South Africa, is facilitating participation alongside the Russian Export Center, Russia’s state-backed institution supporting exports and international business development.
Among the participating organizations is AD SIC >, an industrial association comprised of Russian manufacturers, engineering companies and developers of environmental and heavy industrial technologies. The association has approached the Trade Representation for assistance in establishing direct contact with the African Energy Chamber (AEC) and arranging meetings with its representatives during AEW 2026.
TechEcoMash focuses on ecological engineering technologies for heavy industry, including industrial gas cleaning and air purification systems, waste reduction technologies and equipment designed to improve environmental performance across sectors such as energy, cement and metallurgy. Bringing these businesses together at AEW 2026 strengthens the connections needed to translate industrial capabilities into partnerships that support Africa’s energy and economic development,” says NJ Ayuk, Executive Chairman, AEC.

articles.title: Egypt targets debt reduction to 78% after 5.1% growth: Madbouly - Politics - Egypt - english.ahram.org.eg
articles.summary: Egypt targets debt reduction to 78% after 5.1% growth: Madbouly - Politics - Egypt  english.ahram.org.eg
articles.full_text:
Speaking during President Abdel-Fattah El-Sisi’s meeting with ministers, governors and senior officials, Madbouly said the government was working to turn stronger economic indicators into tangible improvements in prices, services and employment.
The meeting took place on 29 September at the Strategic Command headquarters in the New Capital, attended by military and civilian police commanders, village leaders, experts and specialists.
Madbouly said the government recognized citizens’ concerns despite declining inflation, stronger foreign-currency resources and falling debt ratios. An October conference would present specific budgets and implementation programmes to address public priorities over the next two to three years.
Debt reduction and higher revenues
Madbouly said budget-sector debt fell to approximately 81.8 percent of GDP at the end of FY2025/2026, with the current budget targeting a further decline to around 78 percent.
El-Sisi had directed the government to work towards 75 percent, he added, saying a plan had been drawn up to reduce debt and its servicing costs gradually and sustainably.
Madbouly compared the latest ratio with approximately 96 percent, describing a decline of more than 14 percentage points. Finance ministry documents date the 95.7 percent reading to June 2023, followed by 83.8 percent in June 2025, with 81.8 percent previously projected for June 2026.
Reaching 75 percent would represent an overall reduction of approximately 21 percentage points from the level he cited, Madbouly said.
The previous fiscal year recorded a primary surplus of 4.9 percent of GDP, he added. A primary surplus means budget revenues exceed expenditure before interest payments.
Government revenues increased by 32 percent and tax revenues by approximately 27 percent without raising tax rates, he said, attributing the improvement to a broader tax base, better administration and collection, and more efficient spending.
Lower debt-servicing costs would create greater room for education, healthcare and essential services, Madbouly said. Health allocations rose by approximately 30 percent in FY2026/2027, while education allocations increased by around 20 percent.
External debt falls by $3 billion
Madbouly distinguished external debt owed by budget-sector entities from Egypt’s total external debt, which also includes economic authorities, banks and the private sector.
Budget-sector external debt declined from $79.1 billion two years earlier to $76.1 billion on 30 June 2026, a reduction of $3 billion, he said.
The government plans to reduce this debt by a further $1.5–2 billion annually to ease external repayment obligations, in line with presidential directives.
Remittances reach $35 billion as reserves rise
Madbouly said remittances from Egyptians abroad reached approximately $35 billion between January and August 2026, up 32 percent from the same period a year earlier.
That eight-month figure updates the central bank’s previously announced January–July total of $29.7 billion, which represented growth of 28.1 percent. Remittances reached a record $47.3 billion in FY2025/2026, up 29.6 percent year on year.
Madbouly said tourism continued to expand and Suez Canal revenues had begun recovering, strengthening foreign-currency resources and the economy’s ability to absorb external shocks.
Net international reserves reached approximately $57.2 billion, compared with $49.2 billion a year earlier, an increase of around 16.2 percent, he said.
The central bank’s latest reserve figures put the total at $57.2145 billion at the end of August.
Madbouly stressed that the improvement reflected higher foreign-currency holdings and gains in the value of gold reserves. Foreign-currency holdings themselves increased from approximately $35 billion to nearly $38 billion, he said, despite rising expenditure and repayment commitments.
Stronger foreign-currency resources and economic measures had also helped Egypt absorb sharp price increases, he added.
Growth and foreign investment shift towards industry
Madbouly described Egypt’s 5.1 percent growth rate as among the highest in the Middle East, saying the composition of growth was more significant than the headline figure alone.
Industry, agriculture, communications and information technology, tourism and services were expanding, providing a more sustainable foundation than reliance on Suez Canal revenues or exceptional investment projects, he said.
The latest annual growth figures showed an acceleration from 4.4 percent in FY2024/2025.
Madbouly also highlighted a shift in foreign direct investment towards industrial projects and activities, after investment had previously been more concentrated in oil and gas.
Foreign companies were increasingly establishing factories or expanding existing facilities, he said, attributing the trend to measures that improved the investment climate and simplified procedures.
He said these investments supported local manufacturing, employment and exports.
Declining inflation and better-quality jobs
Madbouly acknowledged that lower inflation had not yet translated into price reductions across many goods.
He cited inflation of 12.7 percent, compared with 23.2 percent in January 2025. The latest nationwide inflation reading stood at 12.7 percent in August.
Maintaining a downward inflation trend would help lower interest rates and support increased production, creating conditions for price reductions, he said. Some commodities had already become cheaper, while others remained a challenge.
Declining inflation means prices rise more slowly; it does not necessarily mean the overall price level has fallen.
Madbouly described unemployment of 5.8 percent as Egypt’s lowest recorded rate, while stressing that the government must focus on jobs offering greater quality, sustainability and income.
The latest quarterly labour figures showed unemployment at 5.8 percent in the second quarter of 2026, down from 6 percent in the preceding quarter.
He said increasing women’s employment and worker productivity remained priorities. Communications and information technology and advanced industries were receiving particular attention because of their potential to provide higher-value employment for young Egyptians.
IMF assessment and global pressures
Madbouly cited the IMF’s recent assessment as evidence that Egypt had withstood regional shocks more effectively than international institutions initially expected.
The IMF’s 21 September Country Focus article, titled “Resilience Under Pressure: Egypt’s Economy Defied Expectations,” credited swift policy responses, stronger economic buffers and exchange-rate flexibility with helping absorb the Middle East war’s repercussions.
However, it also warned that public debt and financing needs remained high and financing relied heavily on short maturities. It called for more decisive reforms and a stronger role for the private sector.
Madbouly said the assessment did not mean Egypt was free of crises. The government understood the remaining challenges and was implementing measures to improve living conditions, including directives issued by El-Sisi during the Prophet’s birthday celebration.
Reflecting on his participation in the United Nations General Assembly in New York, Madbouly said leaders from advanced and emerging economies had highlighted slowing growth, inflation, rising debt and an energy crisis linked to the ongoing war.
He said living costs in some major economies had more than doubled within two years, presenting this as part of his account of discussions at the gathering.
October conference to address public priorities
Madbouly said the forthcoming conference would maximize participation, listen closely to citizens and openly discuss facts, challenges, criticism and questions.
Building on preparations for the October conference, it would explain Egypt’s development path and the government’s assessment of what could have happened without the projects and measures implemented in recent years.
Its principal priority would be to provide clear answers and plans addressing citizens’ concerns over the next two to three years.
Madbouly said specific budgets and implementation programmes would be submitted to El-Sisi for directives to begin execution.
He also said regular meetings with senior officials were particularly important during exceptional circumstances, helping build agreement on policy approaches and clarify responsibilities.

articles.title: South Africa's trade surplus rises by R2.5 billion - IOL
articles.summary: South Africa's trade surplus rises by R2.5 billion  IOL
articles.full_text:
Port of Durban South Africa’s trade surplus widened to R20.5 billion in August as imports fell faster than exports, although higher oil prices could put pressure on the trade balance in coming months.
Image: Leon Lestrade
South Africa’s merchandise trade surplus widened to R20.5 billion in August, from a revised R18.0 billion in July, according to trade data released by the South African Revenue Service (SARS).
The outcome exceeded consensus expectations compiled by Bloomberg.
Investec’s SA Economics unit reported that the improvement was driven by a sharper fall in imports than in exports. Imports declined by R13.7 billion, or 7.8% month-on-month, while exports fell by R11.3 billion, or 5.8%. The net result was an expansion of the merchandise trade surplus.
SARS attributed the decline in export flows largely to lower shipments of platinum group metals, gold, and zinc ores and concentrates. Vegetable product exports also declined by 9.0% month-on-month, while machinery and electronics exports fell by 3.0%.
Platinum group metals remain a significant component of South Africa’s mining basket, accounting for just over 27% of the basket. PGM production contracted by 13.5% year-on-year in July, according to Statistics South Africa.
On the import side, the contraction was partly linked to reduced purchases of petroleum oils excluding crude. Imports of original equipment components and automatic data-processing machines also decreased. These declines more than offset increases in other categories, resulting in a larger monthly fall in the import bill.
Investec cautioned that the relief on the import side may prove temporary. The bank expects import values to rise in the near term as higher energy prices pass through to the trade account. Brent crude oil averaged above US$100 a barrel in September, returning to levels last seen in May amid escalating tensions in the Middle East. Elevated oil prices typically lift the cost of refined petroleum products and related inputs, which form a material share of South Africa’s import basket.
The August figures highlight the competing pressures facing South Africa’s external trade position, with weaker volumes in some key mineral exports offset by a sharp decline in imports.
Investec said the outlook for the trade balance would depend partly on global demand for South African exports, commodity prices and the cost of energy imports.
With oil prices elevated and PGM production still soft, the trajectory of the trade balance in the final quarter will depend on whether export earnings can continue to offset pressure from higher energy and other import costs.

articles.title: Mineral Wealth Conference Calls for Investment, Value Addition to Unlock Mining Potential - Nilepost
articles.summary: Mineral Wealth Conference Calls for Investment, Value Addition to Unlock Mining Potential  Nilepost
articles.full_text:
The Uganda Chamber of Energy and Minerals (UCEM), in partnership with the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development, has called for increased investment, transparent licensing and local value addition to unlock Uganda’s mining potential.
The call was made during the 15th Annual Mineral Wealth Conference held from September 29 to 30 at Speke Resort Munyonyo under the theme, “Beneath the Surface: Unlocking Africa’s Next Mining Powerhouse.”
The conference brought together more than 1,000 delegates from 30 countries, including government officials, mining companies, investors, development partners and innovators. A total of 81 companies exhibited at the event, which also featured business-to-business engagements and a deals room where developers of bankable projects pitched to investors and financiers.
Minister of State for Minerals, Phiona Nyamutoro, said the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development would strengthen its involvement in the conference and focus on ensuring that commitments made during the event translate into action.
“Conferences can only earn their credibility from what happens in the 12 months after they close. And from henceforth, I want to commit on behalf of the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development that we are going to strengthen our involvement in the Mineral Wealth Conference,” Nyamutoro said.
She also said the ministry would review existing mining licences and improve transparency in the licensing process as part of efforts to strengthen investor confidence.
“We will reassure investors to whom we are going to make licensing more transparent and commit to the timelines provided for in the regulation after reviewing all the available licenses,” she said.
UCEM Chief Executive Humphrey Asiimwe said some progress had been made since resolutions reached at the previous conference, including the commencement of operations at the Wagagai gold mine in eastern Uganda.
“Uganda finally also has a large-scale gold mining operation,” Asiimwe said.
He also called for the completion of outstanding regulations under the Mining and Minerals Act 2022.
“We are pushing the ministry to make sure that those come through,” he said.
State Minister for Energy and Mineral Development Sidronius Opolot Okasai said the government wants the minerals sector structured around three key institutions: a policy-making arm within the ministry, an independent regulator and a national mining company.
He said the national mining company was already in place but Uganda still needed a standalone regulator for the minerals sector.
“In energy we have an electricity regulator, in petroleum we have a regulator, and minerals does not have a standalone regulator,” Okasai said.
Development partners also pledged continued support for Uganda’s efforts to formalise mining and improve responsible mineral production.
German Ambassador to Uganda Sigrid Sommer said Germany is supporting Uganda’s mining sector through a project worth more than €6 million focused on responsible mineral sourcing and the formalisation of artisanal and small-scale mining.
“It will take investors willing to commit capital and financial institutions prepared to design products that work for artisanal and small-scale operators, not only large mines,” Sommer said.
EU Ambassador to Uganda Jan Sadak said the European Union was preparing more than €16 million in additional grant funding for Uganda’s mining sector.
The funding would bring the EU’s total mobilisation for the sector to more than €25 million, he said, with a focus on formalising artisanal mining and helping Uganda’s minerals meet international standards.
“Mining needs power, and it needs people. With over €16 million in additional grant funding, the EU will have mobilised more than €25 million in grants for Uganda’s mining sector, helping formalise artisanal miners, many of them women, and preparing Uganda’s minerals to meet international standards,” Sadak said.
State Minister for Science, Technology and Innovation, Eng. Asiimwe Jonard, called for increased local processing of Uganda’s minerals to support industrialisation, employment and technology transfer.
“Uganda cannot continue to export its minerals in raw form. When we do, we deny ourselves industrial development, jobs, technology transfer and government revenue. Our minerals must be processed locally to create more value before they reach international markets,” Asiimwe said.
Ecobank Uganda Managing Director Grace Muliisa, speaking at the conference’s CEO Breakfast, said financial institutions have a key role to play in developing the mining value chain.
She said Uganda would need to channel more domestic savings into processing, manufacturing and infrastructure if the country is to achieve its long-term economic ambitions.
“Mining alone captures only a small portion of the value that minerals create. If Uganda is to grow its economy from about $59 billion to $500 billion by 2040, we must use our growing domestic savings to finance processing, manufacturing and infrastructure, and capture more of the value along the chain,” Muliisa said.
Following the conference, delegates are scheduled to tour mining operations in eastern Uganda, including Wagagai, Tororo Cement and rare earth projects.
The Eastern Uganda Mining Excursion, organised by UCEM from October 1 to 3, will include visits to phosphate, vermiculite, gold and cement operations.

articles.title: BNSF Rail Talk: Capacity Where it Counts: BNSF Completes Major Network Expansion Projects - Railway Track and Structures
articles.summary: BNSF Rail Talk: Capacity Where it Counts: BNSF Completes Major Network Expansion Projects  Railway Track and Structures
articles.full_text:
BNSF Engineering teams recently completed capital expansion projects at three key locations on our network, bringing new capacity to the Midwest, Southwest and Southeast. This new infrastructure will improve network fluidity, increase yard productivity and enable more consistent service for customers.
Galesburg, Illinois
At the Galesburg hump yard, one of our network’s largest and where railcars are sorted into new trains, we’ve added a second parallel lead track to improve productivity and train arrival/departure flexibility. The second track reduces the time between processing trains over the hump because a second inbound train can be readied while cars from the prior train are cut and released.
We also built a connection to the departure tracks on the east side of the yard.
“The way the Galesburg yard was configured results in tracks on the east side of the yard being unable to directly reach the hump crest,” said Craig Rasmussen,assistant vice president of engineering services & structures. “The second lead connects into these tracks, allowing operational flexibility with more tracks available to arriving inbound trains.”
With the upgrade, two additional trains (or about 250 additional railcars) will be processed daily, improving fluidity in and around the terminal and driving more reliable service for our customers.
Work began Dec. 29, 2025, and the first train traversed the new lead track on July 30, more than a month ahead of target.
Winslow, Arizona
At Winslow, our Engineering team completed track improvements that support more efficient locomotive power modifications on our Southern Transcon.
Previously, when power modification work needed to be performed at Winslow, the mainline would be blocked. But now, with this additional track capacity, the work can be done while keeping the mainline clear. Also, by reducing power modification events in other areas of the Southern Transcon, we’ll enhance the movement of all trains and allow for better crew utilization.
Construction started on May 18 and was completed by July 16.
“The success of the Winslow project came from the strong teamwork and communication between multiple departments,” said Travis Shuck, general construction supervisor. “Our field personnel did an outstanding job executing the work safely and professionally while staying focused on the plan. I’m proud of their dedication and commitment to completing this project safely.”
Memphis, Tennessee
In Memphis, we added three new receiving and departure tracks using a former intermodal facility location. The new tracks feed into our hump yard next door. This added track capacity improves processing of increased volume at a critical location.
The installation of these new tracks adds capacity for more than 200 railcars per day.
“This project wasn’t in our original 2026 capital plan,” said Craig Morehouse, executive vice president & chief operations officer. “Volume growth with existing customers and new long-term business opportunities materialized quickly in 2026 and we adjusted to accommodate our customers’ needs.”
Construction began in mid-June. The new tracks were online on Sept. 10, well ahead of the original Nov. 30 projection.
“These projects are great examples of targeted investments that deliver real operational value,” Morehouse said. “We’re creating capacity where we need it, improving fluidity across key parts of the network and giving our teams more flexibility to serve our customers.”

articles.title: African Development Bank and Germany sign pact to boost Africa’s railways - The Eastleigh Voice
articles.summary: African Development Bank and Germany sign pact to boost Africa’s railways  The Eastleigh Voice
articles.full_text:
The African Development Bank Group has signed a letter of intent with the German Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development (BMZ) to cooperate on developing Africa's railway systems and deepening regional economic integration.
The agreement was signed during the inaugural African European Industry Dialogue on Railways, held as part of InnoTrans, the International Trade Fair for Transport Technology in Berlin.
Mike Salawou, the Bank Group's Director for Infrastructure and Urban Development, signed on behalf of the institution. Michael Krake, BMZ's Deputy Director General for Economic Cooperation, signed for Germany. The dialogue was jointly organised by the Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ), Deutsche Bahn, and the EU's Global Gateway initiative.
More To Read
What the partnership will do
Under the agreement, the two entities will work together to reduce Africa's transport costs, improve cross-border interoperability, promote low-carbon transport solutions, embed sustainable transport policies, and build a robust local labour market in the railway sector through skills transfer and vocational training.
Cooperation will begin with a joint feasibility study for an African Rail Competence Centre, to be implemented by GIZ and expected to launch by October 2026. The Centre would bring together innovation and training to modernise and expand Africa's railways.
The scale of the challenge
Africa's rail network represents only 8 to 10 per cent of the world's total. The continent has roughly 90,000 kilometres of railway lines, but much of it is fragmented, ageing, or designed for extraction rather than integration. Colonial-era lines were built to move minerals and agricultural goods from hinterlands to ports—not to connect African countries.
Different gauges, poor maintenance, and missing links mean that a train from Mombasa cannot easily reach Kigali, and a wagon from Lobito cannot roll seamlessly into Lusaka.
The African Continental Free Trade Area, which creates a market of over 1.4 billion people, is driving growing demand for cross-border freight and passenger movement. But without functional railways, that demand will be met by trucks on roads that are often congested, costly, and unsafe. Road transport accounts for 80 to 90 per cent of freight movement in Africa, compared with 20 to 30 per cent in Europe and the United States.
The bank's portfolio
In his keynote address, Salawou pointed to the Bank's existing investments in the Lobito Corridor, the Standard Gauge Railway programme in East Africa, the Nacala Corridor, Algeria's North-South Rail Corridor, Morocco's high-speed rail system, and urban rail projects in Senegal and Nigeria.
The Lobito Corridor—a 1,300-kilometre railway linking Angola's Atlantic coast to the mineral belts of the DRC and Zambia—has become a flagship for Western infrastructure engagement in Africa. The United States and the European Union have both backed the project, seeing it as a counterweight to Chinese infrastructure dominance on the continent.
The Standard Gauge Railway in Kenya, meanwhile, has been a model and a cautionary tale. It transformed connectivity between Mombasa and Nairobi, but its cost, debt burden, and limited extension have raised questions about sustainability.
The five priorities
Salawou set out five priorities for the sector: a continental market driven by AfCFTA, modal-shift reforms, interoperable standards, financing that crowds in private capital, and the competencies needed to operate the networks once built.
"Building a railway is half the job," he said. "Running it is the harder half."
That line captures the essence of the challenge. Africa has no shortage of railway ambitions. It has a shortage of functioning railways. The difference lies not in construction but in maintenance, operations, regulation, and skills.
What Germany brings
Krake emphasised BMZ's long-standing commitment to supporting Africa's development. "BMZ is committed to working with our African partners to strengthen regional connectivity and support sustainable economic development," he said. "Together with the African Development Bank, we will advance practical cooperation on interoperability, skills development and other priorities that help build a stronger railway sector."
Germany brings technical expertise, vocational training models, and financing. The EU's Global Gateway initiative—Europe's answer to China's Belt and Road—provides the broader strategic framework.

articles.title: What I See For Nigeria Between October 2026 & October 2027 By Dr. Iyanda Ibadan | AstroDu - PM Parrot
articles.summary: What I See For Nigeria Between October 2026 & October 2027 By Dr. Iyanda Ibadan | AstroDu  PM Parrot
articles.full_text:
Happy Independence Day, Nigeria. Today, October 1, 2026, Nigeria marks 66 years of independence.
I have spent considerable time studying the pattern surrounding Nigeria from this Independence Day to the next. I have also compared what I found with what is already happening in the country—the economy, government finances, politics, security, young people, technology and the approaching 2027 general election.
I won’t tell Nigerians that everything will suddenly become fine because today is Independence Day.
I also won’t tell you that Nigeria is about to collapse simply because frightening predictions travel faster on social media.
What I see is more complicated than either story.
Nigeria has entered a year of reckoning, correction and consequence.
Government will be judged increasingly by what it completes, not what it announces. Money will become an even bigger national argument. Young Nigerians will move closer to the centre of economic and political power. Political alliances will change. Courts and other institutions will face difficult tests. Hidden weaknesses will become harder to keep hidden.
But perhaps the biggest question of the next twelve months is remarkably simple:
Can the improvement government says is happening in the economy finally become something ordinary Nigerians can actually feel?
President Bola Tinubu addressed the country this morning under the theme “From Reform to Prosperity.” He argued that Nigeria has passed through the harshest stage of economic reform and must now convert stability into prosperity people can experience. His own definition was practical: affordable food and transportation, reliable electricity, productive work for young Nigerians, access to credit, safer farming and better opportunities for families. (State House Abuja)
That brings us directly to the central issue I see.
Nigeria’s next twelve months are not merely asking whether the economy can improve.
They are asking:
WHEN WILL NIGERIANS FEEL THE IMPROVEMENT?
Because an economy recovering in Abuja and a family recovering in Agege, Aba, Kano, Ibadan or Port Harcourt are not necessarily the same thing.
⸻
FIRST, WHERE DOES NIGERIA REALLY STAND?
There is genuine evidence of economic improvement.
The National Bureau of Statistics reports that real GDP grew 3.89% year-on-year in the first quarter of 2026, against 3.13% in the same quarter of 2025. Manufacturing grew 3.29%, trade grew 2.08%, and the non-oil economy accounted for 96.08% of real GDP. (Nigerian States)
The President said this morning that growth has since moved above 4% this year. That is the government’s current assessment; the NBS website currently still prominently displays its Q1 figures, so I make that distinction deliberately rather than mixing the two numbers together. (State House Abuja)
Inflation has fallen substantially. NBS currently reports headline inflation at 15.39% and food inflation at 19.57%. (Nigerian States)
The Central Bank has also reset its Monetary Policy Rate to 23% following its September 21–22 meeting. (Central Bank of Nigeria)
And yet none of these figures settles the argument around the Nigerian dining table.
A government official can correctly say inflation has fallen.
A woman pricing food in the market can correctly say food is still too expensive.
Both can be telling the truth.
Because falling inflation does not mean prices have returned to where they were. It means the general rate at which prices are increasing has slowed.
That difference will become politically important.
Nigerians don’t eat GDP. No.
They experience an economy through food, rent, transportation, electricity, medication, school fees, interest on loans, the availability of work and whatever remains after the month’s bills have been paid.
That is where the real economic verdict will be delivered.
⸻
THIS IS AN ACCOUNTABILITY YEAR
The first major message I see concerns government itself.
Nigeria is entering a period when implementation becomes more important than announcement.
There will still be launches, speeches, budgets, memoranda, committees and promises.
But the public mood will increasingly ask a less glamorous question:
What was actually completed?
That question will follow roads.
Power.
Agriculture.
Housing.
Security.
Healthcare.
Education.
Employment programmes.
Government revenue.
Public infrastructure.
And something happened yesterday that makes this theme almost impossible to ignore.
On September 30, President Tinubu signed another amendment extending implementation of the 2025 budget until December 31, 2026, specifically giving ministries, departments and agencies additional time to complete ongoing capital projects. (State House Abuja)
Meanwhile, the 2026 Appropriation Act itself provides for ₦68.32 trillion in expenditure, including ₦15.8 trillion for debt service and ₦32.2 trillion for the Development Fund for Capital Expenditure. (State House Abuja)
So there is something Nigerians should understand.
Some of the biggest stories of the coming year will not actually begin in the coming year.
They will be old matters returning because they were never properly settled.
Old projects.
Old obligations.
Old contracts.
Old political grievances.
Old court cases.
Old security problems.
Old debts.
Old promises.
Nigeria will spend part of this cycle meeting yesterday at the door.
And yesterday will be asking for payment.
⸻
MONEY WILL BE ONE OF THE GREAT BATTLEGROUNDS
I cannot overstate how strongly money runs through this period.
Revenue.
Taxes.
Debt.
Banking.
Investment.
Foreign exchange.
Public expenditure.
Contracts.
Borrowing.
Household purchasing power.
Nigeria is moving through a deep financial restructuring.
Some of it is necessary.
More economic activity will become visible to government.
Tax administration will become increasingly digital.
Revenue collection will become more sophisticated.
Leakages will attract attention.
Financial institutions will continue adapting to tighter regulation and recapitalisation.
But the uncomfortable side of the story is financial opacity.
Large numbers will be announced.
Revenue improvements will be announced.
Investments will be announced.
Loans will be announced.
Projects will be announced.
The public question will increasingly be:
Where is the money?
That question does not mean every government figure is false.
It means Nigerians will increasingly demand a connection between the figure announced and the result delivered.
If revenue improves, what changed?
If borrowing increases, what was built?
If investment arrives, where are the jobs?
If GDP expands, whose income expanded with it?
If billions are allocated, where is the completed project?
This year puts unusual pressure on the distance between financial presentation and financial reality.
I expect serious arguments around taxation, revenue, public expenditure and borrowing.
I expect scrutiny around major contracts and financing arrangements.
And I would not be surprised if a significant financial institution, revenue mechanism, major contract, public-finance arrangement or economic deal is forced through uncomfortable investigation, restructuring or public scrutiny.
Somebody may eventually have to open books that were not meant for everybody to read.
⸻
FOLLOW THE MONEY BEHIND THE MONEY
There is an even deeper layer.
Nigeria should pay attention not merely to money that is visible, but to ownership and financial relationships that are difficult to see.
Who ultimately owns what?
Who benefits from a contract?
Who stands behind a company?
Where does extracted wealth end up?
Who finances a network?
Who receives payment after the public-facing company receives payment?
This is where procurement chains, beneficial ownership, tax avoidance, revenue leakages, illegal extraction, oil theft and unexplained financial relationships become important.
I am not accusing a particular person or institution of wrongdoing.
I am saying the coming period is unusually unfriendly to arrangements that depend upon remaining hidden.
Some secrets survive because nobody looks.
Others survive because the people looking are afraid.
This is a year in which both conditions can change.
⸻
DEBT WILL NOT QUIETLY DISAPPEAR
Nigeria’s public debt remains a serious national consideration. The Debt Management Office’s latest published position covers June 30, 2026. (Debt Management Office )
But simply shouting “debt” does not tell us enough.
A country can borrow and become more productive.
A country can also borrow and leave future generations with obligations without creating enough productive assets to service them.
The proper questions are:
What was borrowed?
At what cost?
In what currency?
For how long?
What was the money used for?
And what will exist when repayment becomes due?
That is why I expect increasing scrutiny of loans, concessions, public-private partnerships and foreign financing arrangements.
Some will be useful.
Some may look much better at the signing ceremony than they look after Nigerians read the obligations.
The message here is simple:
Read the fine print.
Nigeria must learn to negotiate as a country that knows its value.
⸻
THE COST OF LIVING REMAINS THE REAL REFERENDUM
Inflation at 15.39% is substantially better than the levels Nigerians endured before.
Food inflation at 19.57% also tells us why relief can still feel distant. (Nigerian States)
The trader doesn’t restock at yesterday’s price because somebody announced a better inflation figure.
The salary earner doesn’t recover purchasing power automatically.
The small business still calculates power, transport, rent, wages and replacement costs.
The family still knows what school fees cost.
So I expect an increasingly sharp argument between macro-economic success and lived economic experience.
Government will point to improving indicators.
Critics will point to continuing hardship.
Neither side should be allowed to win the argument simply by shouting louder.
Look at the evidence.
And then look at people’s lives.
⸻
YOUNG NIGERIAN

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaks during the 62nd Munich Security Conference (MSC) on February 14, 2026 in Munich, southern Germany. Heads of state and government as well as foreign and defence ministers from all over the world are expected to attend the security policy talks from February 13 to 15, 2026. (Photo by THOMAS KIENZLE / AFP)
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has congratulated Nigeria on its 66th Independence Anniversary, describing the country as vital to Africa’s stability and economic growth.
Rubio, in a National Day message released by the U.S. Department of State on Thursday, said Washington valued its strong bilateral relationship with Nigeria.
He also welcomed the substantive dialogue between both countries over the past year.
“On behalf of the United States of America, I extend my congratulations to the people of Nigeria on the 66th anniversary of Nigeria’s independence,” Rubio said.
“The United States places great value on this strong bilateral relationship and appreciates the substantive dialogue undertaken over the past year.”
Rubio highlighted Nigeria’s strategic importance to the continent, citing its democratic standing, economic strength and role in regional affairs.
“As Africa’s largest democracy and one of its largest economies, Nigeria plays a vital role in advancing regional stability and economic growth,” he said.
“The United States is proud to stand alongside Nigeria in pursuit of these common goals.”
He identified democratic principles, religious freedom, expanding commercial relations, peace and security as key pillars of cooperation between Abuja and Washington.
“Our two nations are bound by a shared commitment to continued progress on our common priorities,” he said.
He said the priorities were rooted in “mutual democratic principles, the protection of religious freedom, a growing commercial relationship, and a commitment to fostering peace and security.”
The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that Nigeria-U.S. relations have spanned more than six decades, dating back to Nigeria’s independence from Britain on Oct. 1, 1960.
The United States formally recognised Nigeria on Independence Day, with diplomatic relations between the two countries established on the same day.
Over the years, cooperation has expanded across security, governance, health, trade, investment, technology, energy and people-to-people relations.
The U.S.-Nigeria Binational Commission has provided a platform for coordinating high-level engagements between the two governments.
Its areas of cooperation have included shared prosperity, security, democracy and governance, health, and movement of people.
Rubio reaffirmed the U.S. commitment to working alongside Nigeria in pursuit of shared economic, democratic and security objectives.
He concluded the Independence Day message with wishes for peace, unity, prosperity and hope for Nigerians.
“Congratulations once again. May this proud nation and its people thrive in peace, unity, prosperity, and hope for generations to come,” the Secretary of State said.
